q: Mark and Nora file jointly and have two qualifying children, ages 6 and 9. Their modified AGI is $412,500. Assume the child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child and is reduced by $50 for each $1,000 (or fraction thereof) of modified AGI above $400,000. What is their child tax credit?
exp: The excess of $12,500 is rounded up to 13 increments of $1,000, so the reduction is 13 x $50 = $650 and the credit is $4,400 - $650 = $3,750. Using 12.5 increments without rounding up gives $3,775.

q: Opal and Paul file jointly. Their dependents are their son, age 16; their daughter, who turned 17 in November; and Paul's widowed mother, who lives with them. Assume the child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child, the credit for other dependents is $500 per dependent, and their AGI is well below the phase-out threshold. What is their total child tax credit and credit for other dependents?
exp: Only a child under 17 at year-end is a qualifying child for the child tax credit ($2,200); the 17-year-old and the mother each generate the $500 credit for other dependents: $2,200 + $500 + $500 = $3,200. Counting the 17-year-old as a qualifying child gives $4,900.

q: Rick and Sue file jointly and paid $7,000 of qualifying child care for their two children, ages 3 and 5, so they could work. Rick earned $40,000 and Sue earned $5,000 from part-time work. Assume the expense limit is $6,000 for two or more qualifying persons and the applicable credit percentage is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
exp: Qualifying expenses are limited to the lesser of actual costs, the $6,000 cap, or the lower-earning spouse's earned income ($5,000), so the credit is 20% x $5,000 = $1,000. Ignoring the earned income limit gives $1,200.

q: Ted and Uma, who file jointly, paid $8,000 of graduate tuition for each of their two children during the year. Their AGI is below the phase-out range. Assume the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses. What is their maximum lifetime learning credit?
exp: The lifetime learning credit is computed per taxpayer return, not per student: 20% x the $10,000 cap = $2,000. Applying the cap to each student separately gives $3,200.

q: Which of the following statements about the American opportunity tax credit is correct?
choices: It may be claimed for any number of years of postsecondary education
Its maximum is a single amount per taxpayer regardless of the number of eligible students
Up to 40% of the credit may be refundable
It applies to graduate school tuition after the first four years of postsecondary education
exp: Up to 40% of the American opportunity credit is refundable. The credit is computed per eligible student and is limited to the first four years of postsecondary education; the per-return cap and unlimited years describe the lifetime learning credit.

q: Vera's U.S. tax liability before credits is $30,000 on worldwide taxable income of $150,000, of which $50,000 is foreign-source taxable income. She paid $12,000 of foreign income taxes. What is Vera's foreign tax credit for the year?
exp: The credit is limited to U.S. tax x foreign-source taxable income / worldwide taxable income: $30,000 x $50,000 / $150,000 = $10,000; the $2,000 excess carries back one year and forward ten. Crediting all $12,000 ignores the §904 limitation.

q: Wendy has a qualifying child and earned income that would otherwise entitle her to the earned income credit. She also has $12,500 of interest and dividend income. Assume the disqualified investment income limit for the year is $11,950. What earned income credit may Wendy claim?
choices: $0, because her investment income exceeds the limit
The full credit computed from her earned income
The credit reduced by the $550 of investment income over the limit
50% of the credit computed from her earned income
exp: If disqualified investment income exceeds the annual limit by any amount, no earned income credit is allowed; it is a cliff, not a phase-out. Reducing the credit by the excess treats the rule as a phase-out.

q: Xena, whose AGI qualifies her for a 20% retirement savings contributions (saver's) credit rate, contributed $2,500 to her traditional IRA. Assume the credit applies to a maximum of $2,000 of contributions per person, and she received no retirement distributions. What is her saver's credit?
exp: The credit is the applicable rate times contributions up to the $2,000 cap: 20% x $2,000 = $400. Applying 20% to the full $2,500 contribution gives $500.

q: Which of the following individual credits is refundable?
choices: The child and dependent care credit
The lifetime learning credit
The earned income credit
The foreign tax credit
exp: The earned income credit is refundable, so it can produce a refund in excess of tax liability. The dependent care, lifetime learning and foreign tax credits are nonrefundable (the foreign tax credit has carryovers instead).

q: During the year Yolanda earned wages of $120,000 from one employer and $90,000 from a second, unrelated employer, and each employer withheld 6.2% Social Security tax on all wages paid. Assume the Social Security wage base is $176,100. What credit for excess Social Security tax withheld can Yolanda claim on her return?
exp: Total withheld is $7,440 + $5,580 = $13,020, but the maximum employee tax is 6.2% x $176,100 = $10,918.20, so $2,101.80 is credited on her return. Each employer withheld correctly, but the excess arises from combining two employers' wages.

q: Zeke, a single taxpayer, has alternative minimum taxable income of $600,000. Assume the AMT exemption is $90,000, reduced by 50% of AMTI in excess of $500,000. What is Zeke's AMT exemption?
exp: The exemption is reduced by 50% x ($600,000 - $500,000) = $50,000, leaving $40,000. Using a 25% phase-out rate gives $65,000.

q: Abe itemizes. His taxable income is $200,000 after deducting state and local taxes of $10,000, qualified home acquisition mortgage interest of $15,000 and charitable contributions of $8,000. He also received $5,000 of tax-exempt interest on specified private activity bonds. He has no other adjustments or preferences. What is Abe's alternative minimum taxable income before the exemption?
exp: For AMT, state and local taxes are added back ($10,000) and private activity bond interest is a preference ($5,000): $200,000 + $15,000 = $215,000. Qualified acquisition mortgage interest and charitable contributions remain deductible, so adding them back gives $238,000.

q: Beth, a single taxpayer, claimed a $15,000 standard deduction and reported taxable income of $100,000. She has no other AMT adjustments or preferences. What is her alternative minimum taxable income before the exemption?
exp: The standard deduction is not allowed in computing AMTI, so it is added back: $100,000 + $15,000 = $115,000. Assuming a taxpayer who does not itemize has no AMT adjustments gives $100,000.

q: Carl exercised incentive stock options to buy 1,000 shares of his employer's stock at $10 per share when the stock was worth $35 per share. He held the shares at year-end. What is Carl's AMT adjustment for the year from this exercise?
exp: No regular tax income arises on exercise of an ISO, but the bargain element is a positive AMT adjustment: ($35 - $10) x 1,000 = $25,000. The $0 answer is the regular tax result only.

q: Two years after exercising incentive stock options for 1,000 shares at $10 per share when the stock was worth $35 per share (and reporting the related AMT adjustment), Carl sold the shares for $50 per share in a qualifying disposition. What gain does Carl report for regular tax and for AMT purposes in the year of sale?
choices: $40,000 regular tax gain; $15,000 AMT gain
$40,000 gain for both regular tax and AMT
$15,000 regular tax gain; $40,000 AMT gain
$15,000 gain for both regular tax and AMT
exp: Regular tax basis is the $10 exercise price, giving a $40,000 gain, while AMT basis includes the $25,000 adjustment ($35 per share), giving a $15,000 AMT gain (a $25,000 negative adjustment). Using the same basis for both double-counts the earlier AMT adjustment.

q: Which of the following AMT items can give rise to a minimum tax credit usable against regular tax in later years?
choices: The bargain element on exercise of an incentive stock option
The add-back of state and local taxes
Tax-exempt interest on specified private activity bonds
The add-back of the standard deduction
exp: The minimum tax credit arises only from deferral items, such as the ISO adjustment, which reverses when the stock is sold. Exclusion items such as the taxes add-back, private activity bond interest and standard deduction never reverse and create no credit.

q: Which of the following creates an AMT depreciation adjustment for property placed in service this year?
choices: Straight-line MACRS on a commercial building
Bonus depreciation on qualifying equipment
200% declining-balance MACRS on 7-year equipment, with no bonus depreciation claimed
Straight-line MACRS on residential rental property
exp: For AMT, personal property depreciated at 200% declining balance must use 150% declining balance, creating an adjustment. Straight-line real property depreciation and bonus depreciation are allowed the same for AMT, so they create no adjustment.

q: Dee, a single taxpayer, has AMTI of $300,000 and regular tax of $50,000. Assume her AMT exemption is $90,000 with no phase-out at her income level, the AMT rate is 26% on the first $239,100 of the AMT base and 28% above that, and she has no capital gains or AMT foreign tax credit. What is Dee's alternative minimum tax?
exp: The AMT base is $300,000 - $90,000 = $210,000, all taxed at 26%, so tentative minimum tax is $54,600 and AMT is the $4,600 excess over regular tax. The $54,600 figure is tentative minimum tax, not the additional AMT owed.

q: Earl has one qualifying child, earned income of $12,500 and a regular tax liability of $0. Assume the refundable additional child tax credit equals 15% of earned income over $2,500, limited to $1,700 per qualifying child. What refundable child tax credit may Earl claim?
exp: The refundable portion is the lesser of $1,700 or 15% x ($12,500 - $2,500) = $1,500. Claiming the $1,700 maximum ignores the earned income formula.

q: Fran and her husband both work full time and have a 10-year-old son. Which of the following payments is a qualifying expense for the child and dependent care credit?
choices: Overnight summer camp for the son
Private school tuition for the son's fifth-grade year
Day camp for the son while both parents work
Payments to their 17-year-old daughter to babysit the son
exp: Day camp for a child under 13 that enables the parents to work qualifies. Overnight camp and kindergarten-or-higher tuition do not, and payments to the taxpayer's own child under age 19 are excluded.

q: Gus, a first-year college student whose parents claim him as a dependent, paid $1,500 of tuition to the college and $600 for required textbooks he bought online, plus $5,000 for a dormitory room. His parents' AGI is below the phase-out range. Assume the American opportunity credit equals 100% of the first $2,000 of qualified expenses plus 25% of the next $2,000. What American opportunity credit may his parents claim?
exp: Qualified expenses include tuition and required course materials even if not bought from the school ($2,100), but not room and board: $2,000 + 25% x $100 = $2,025. Excluding the textbooks gives $1,500.

q: Hana, a single taxpayer, would qualify for a $2,500 American opportunity credit before any phase-out. Her modified AGI is $84,000. Assume the credit phases out ratably for single filers with modified AGI between $80,000 and $90,000. What is her allowable credit?
exp: Modified AGI is 40% through the $10,000 phase-out range, so the credit is $2,500 x 60% = $1,500. The $1,000 figure is the disallowed amount.

q: Ian earned $60,000 in wages. His wife was a full-time student for nine months of the year and had no earnings. They paid $4,000 of qualifying care for their one child and file jointly. Assume the expense limit for one qualifying person is $3,000, a full-time student spouse is deemed to earn $250 per month with one qualifying person, and the credit rate is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
exp: The student spouse's deemed earned income is $250 x 9 = $2,250, which caps qualifying expenses: 20% x $2,250 = $450. Using the $3,000 expense limit ignores the earned income limitation.

q: Jill paid $1,000 of foreign income tax on foreign investment income. Her marginal U.S. tax rate is 24%, and the foreign tax credit limitation is not a factor. By how much more does claiming the foreign tax credit reduce her U.S. tax than deducting the foreign tax as an itemized deduction?
exp: A credit reduces tax dollar for dollar ($1,000), while a deduction saves only 24% x $1,000 = $240, a difference of $760. The $240 figure is the value of the deduction, not the difference.

q: Kim and Lou, who both work, paid $8,000 of qualifying day care for their two young children. Kim excluded $5,000 under her employer's dependent care assistance program. Assume the expense limit for two qualifying persons is $6,000 and the credit rate is 20%. What is their child and dependent care credit?
exp: The $6,000 limit is reduced by the $5,000 excluded under the employer plan, leaving $1,000 x 20% = $200. Applying 20% to the $3,000 of expenses not reimbursed gives $600, which ignores the reduction of the cap.

q: Which statement about net capital gain under the individual alternative minimum tax is correct?
choices: Net capital gain is taxed at the 26% and 28% AMT rates
Net capital gain is excluded from AMTI
Net capital gain is added back as a tax preference item
Qualified dividends and net capital gain keep the same preferential rates under the AMT as under the regular tax
exp: The AMT computation taxes net capital gain and qualified dividends at the same 0/15/20% rates used for regular tax, with only the remaining AMT base taxed at 26%/28%. Net capital gain is included in AMTI, not excluded or treated as a preference.

q: Mia and Ned file jointly with AGI below all phase-out ranges. Their daughter, a first-year undergraduate, had $4,000 of qualified tuition, and Ned took a graduate course costing $5,000. Assume the American opportunity credit is 100% of the first $2,000 plus 25% of the next $2,000 per student, and the lifetime learning credit is 20% of up to $10,000 of expenses. What is their maximum total education credit?
exp: Different credits may be claimed for different students in the same year: an American opportunity credit of $2,500 for the daughter plus a lifetime learning credit of 20% x $5,000 = $1,000 for Ned, for $3,500. Using only the lifetime learning credit on all $9,000 gives $1,800.

q: Opal's regular tax liability before credits is $1,200, and she qualifies for a $2,000 lifetime learning credit. She has no other credits. What is the result?
choices: Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is lost
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is refunded
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is carried forward
Her tax is reduced to $0 and the $800 excess is carried back one year
exp: The lifetime learning credit is nonrefundable and has no carryover, so it can reduce tax only to zero and the excess is lost. Refund treatment applies only to refundable credits such as the earned income credit.

q: Pete exercised nonqualified stock options and acquired employer stock with a $25,000 spread between fair market value and exercise price. The stock had a readily ascertainable value. How is the exercise treated?
choices: $25,000 of ordinary income for regular tax and a $25,000 positive AMT adjustment
No regular tax income and a $25,000 positive AMT adjustment
No income for regular tax or AMT until the shares are sold
$25,000 of ordinary income for regular tax and no AMT adjustment
exp: The spread on a nonqualified option is compensation income on exercise under §83 for both regular tax and AMT, so no AMT adjustment is needed. The positive AMT adjustment with no regular income describes an incentive stock option.

q: Quinn, a U.S. citizen working abroad, earned $150,000 of foreign wages, of which he excluded $130,000 under the foreign earned income exclusion. He paid $30,000 of foreign income tax on the wages. Assume the overall foreign tax credit limitation is not binding. What foreign tax credit may Quinn claim?
exp: No credit is allowed for foreign taxes allocable to excluded income, so only $30,000 x $20,000 / $150,000 = $4,000 is creditable. Claiming the full $30,000 would give a double benefit on the excluded wages.
